blockMcqs.question: Why is the rate limiter an expert-level LLD problem?
options: It requires a database migration
Picking the right algorithm and making updates thread-safe are hard
It only tests knowledge of HTTP status codes
It has no interface design involved
blockMcqs.explanation: The snapshot card says the hard part is choosing an algorithm with the right memory/accuracy trade-off and making the counter update thread-safe under concurrency.

blockMcqs.question: Which of these is a functional requirement for the rate limiter?
options: The check must run in O(1) time
Reject requests beyond the limit per key
Memory per key must stay bounded
The system must be thread-safe
blockMcqs.explanation: Rejecting requests beyond the limit is a functional requirement; overhead, memory, and thread-safety are non-functional requirements covered separately.

blockMcqs.question: What does the shared "decides allow or reject" verb become in the design?
options: A field on RateLimitConfig
A single allow(key) method on the RateLimiter interface
A separate class per algorithm with no shared contract
An enum value
blockMcqs.explanation: The card explains that the shared decision behavior becomes one allow(key) method on the RateLimiter interface so callers stay algorithm-agnostic.

blockMcqs.question: How does token bucket compute refill without a background timer?
options: It polls a cron job every second
Lazily, from elapsed time times refill rate on each request
It never refills once created
A separate thread refills each bucket
blockMcqs.explanation: The card notes refill is usually computed lazily on each request using elapsed time multiplied by rate, avoiding a background timer per bucket.

blockMcqs.question: What is the boundary burst problem in fixed window counters?
options: Counters never reset between windows
A client can send 2x the limit across a window boundary
The counter overflows after one request
It only affects the first window ever created
blockMcqs.explanation: Because windows don't overlap, a client can send the full limit right before and right after a boundary, doubling the intended rate briefly.

blockMcqs.question: How does sliding window counter estimate the current rate?
options: It stores every request timestamp
currentWindowCount plus previousWindowCount times overlap fraction
It ignores the previous window entirely
It doubles the fixed window limit
blockMcqs.explanation: The formula weights the previous window's count by how much it overlaps the current sliding view, approximating an exact sliding window at O(1) memory.

blockMcqs.question: Which algorithm has memory usage that grows with request volume?
options: Token Bucket
Fixed Window
Sliding Window Log
Sliding Window Counter
blockMcqs.explanation: The compare table shows Sliding Window Log stores a timestamp per request up to the limit, so its memory scales with traffic unlike the O(1) alternatives.

blockMcqs.question: In the TokenBucketLimiter pseudocode, what happens when tokens < 1?
options: The bucket capacity is increased
allow() returns false and no token is deducted
The key is permanently blocked
It waits until a token appears
blockMcqs.explanation: The code checks if bucket.tokens >= 1 before deducting; otherwise it returns false immediately without blocking or mutating state further.

blockMcqs.question: In SlidingWindowCounterLimiter, when does previousCount get updated?
options: On every single request
When elapsed time in the current window exceeds windowSeconds
Only when the limit is exceeded
It is never updated after creation
blockMcqs.explanation: The pseudocode rolls currentCount into previousCount and resets currentCount only once the current window's elapsed time passes windowSeconds.

blockMcqs.question: Which pattern does the RateLimiter interface and its implementations represent?
options: Singleton
Strategy
Observer
Decorator
blockMcqs.explanation: TokenBucketLimiter, SlidingWindowCounterLimiter, and FixedWindowLimiter are interchangeable implementations of one interface picked at construction — the Strategy pattern.

blockMcqs.question: What race condition can push a key over its limit?
options: A missing RateLimitConfig field
Check-then-act: two requests both read old state then both write
Using Strategy pattern instead of Factory
Storing config in the wrong class
blockMcqs.explanation: Two concurrent requests can both read "tokens available" before either writes back the decrement, letting both through over the limit — a check-then-act race.

blockMcqs.question: Why does an in-process PerKeyStore fail behind a load balancer?
options: It runs out of memory instantly
Each server enforces its own separate quota, multiplying the real limit
It cannot store timestamps
Redis is required even for a single server
blockMcqs.explanation: With N servers each holding independent in-memory state, the effective limit becomes N times the intended value since no server sees the others' counts.
